title: Data Splitting and Leakage Prevention
learning_outcomes: Explain data Splitting and Leakage Prevention and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in data Splitting and Leakage Prevention to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study data Splitting and Leakage Prevention within Data Fundamentals and Preparation. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Data quality and governance shape downstream outcomes. Record where data came from, what it means, and how it was transformed before training.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Training, validation, and test sets serve different roles. Keep related examples or future observations separated when necessary; data leakage makes offline results look better than the model’s true generalization.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Training, validation, and test datasets
items.text: Training data fits the model, validation data guides choices, and a held-out test estimates final performance. Reusing the test set to repeatedly tune decisions turns it into part of the development process.

items.title: Random and stratified splitting
items.text: Random and stratified splitting is one of the concepts used to reason about data splitting and leakage prevention. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Data leakage scenarios
items.text: Leakage occurs when training or model selection uses information unavailable at the intended prediction time or information from evaluation data. It can produce deceptively strong offline results.

content_blocks.code:
rows = [{"id": 1, "score": 8}, {"id": 2, "score": None}, {"id": 2, "score": 6}]
seen = set()
clean = []
for row in rows:
    if row["id"] in seen or row["score"] is None:
        continue
    seen.add(row["id"])
    clean.append(row)
print("kept rows:", len(clean))

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
